entry.title: perf(subtitles): vectorise the geometry extraction's two per-pixel loops
entry.content:
perf(subtitles): vectorise the geometry extraction's two per-pixel loops

`_collect_layer` and `_blit_coverage` walked one Python iteration per painted
pixel of every glyph. Together they were the geometry render: 11.19 ms of an
11.53 ms extraction, against libass's own render at 0.07 ms.

That cost is why the color arrives late. A cue's measurement ran ~27 ms in the
field, above the rate cues arrive at, so the lookahead queue overflowed — 18 of
31 prefetched renders dropped, 1 prefetch entry retained, and only 25 of 48
native draws had boxes to color.

Measured on the same synthetic cue (M3 Pro, 24 tokens, 1920x1080, 40 reps):

    collect layers   11.192 -> 0.517 ms   21.6x
    coverage masks    3.961 -> 0.077 ms   51.4x
    owners alloc      0.111 -> 0.019 ms    5.8x
    measure one cue  11.620 -> 0.734 ms   15.8x

The engine comparison inverts with it: native's in-process work was 1.25x the
legacy renderer's and is now 0.085x.

`owners` becomes a numpy array rather than `array("H")`; numpy is already a
dependency of this package (`overpaint` uses it).

Two behavioural notes, both deliberate:

The refusals are unchanged in meaning and widened in scope — they test a whole
layer rather than stopping at its first offending pixel. On failure the partial
accumulator therefore differs, and nothing reads it: `resolve_outcome` discards
the render either way.

`_blit_coverage`'s offsets are routinely NEGATIVE. The crop is the token's INK
and a bitmap's origin sits above and left of its ink whenever the glyph has
bearing, which is most glyphs. The first draft sliced with them unclipped, and a
negative slice start counts from the far end — so the window came back empty and
the layer's coverage was dropped silently. The differential test missed it by
cropping to the bitmap rect, where the offsets are always zero; it now derives
the crop from painted pixels the way production does, and the case is pinned.

The differential runs the old implementation beside the new one over 500 seeded
layer sets. Seeded rather than Hypothesis: this package ships independently and
its dev group is `pytest` alone, so a property-testing dependency here is a
distribution decision this test does not need to make.

entry.title: test(bench): cover the engine comparison, and correct a claim the fie…
entry.content:
test(bench): cover the engine comparison, and correct a claim the field refuted

`benchmark_engines` landed in d4109b7a by accident — `git add -A` on the
regression fix swept it in, so that commit carries a change its message does not
mention. Not rewriting a pushed branch to tidy that; recording it here instead,
and adding the tests it should have arrived with. Every other leg of this
benchmark has a guard that it measured something; this one had none.

Also corrects the comment beside `subtitle_draw`'s token count. It asserted the
legacy renderer "produces its own boxes rather than consuming measured ones",
which a session with both engines refutes: 6 of 36 legacy draws carried measured
boxes and 25 of 48 native ones did. Geometry runs on both paths — it feeds hover
and scanning regardless of who draws — so the boxes report what happened to have
landed, not what the cue holds. The change itself stands; only its reason was
too absolute.

entry.title: fix(telemetry): teach the sink the extraction metrics it now receives
entry.content:
fix(telemetry): teach the sink the extraction metrics it now receives

The extraction split broke subtitles outright. `_GeometryTelemetry.record` raises
on a metric name it does not know — deliberately, so a typo cannot vanish — and
`resolve_outcome` catches `Exception` and reports `provider-error`. So four new
timing calls inside `extract_token_geometry` did not degrade telemetry: they
failed EVERY geometry render, and a live session had no hit boxes, no color and
no scanning. The legacy renderer kept working, because it never asks for geometry.

Field evidence (report 20260908-215427, build gb5622129): 8 of 8
`subtitle_geometry_render` spans `outcome=failed error_code=provider-error`,
`subtitle_geometry.completed=0`, and `measured_boxes=0` on every native draw.

The four histograms are registered and mapped now. The real fix is the gate: this
is a contract with an enforcing end and an enumerable one, and nothing bound them
— `NullTelemetry` and every test collector accept any name, so both halves of the
suite passed while the pair was broken. `GEOMETRY_METRICS` makes the library's
side enumerable and `test_geometry_telemetry_contract` asserts the application's
sink accepts all of it, with a negative control that the map still refuses an
unknown name. Removing the four entries again turns exactly those cases red.

Worth stating plainly: a telemetry name mismatch taking down rendering is a
disproportionate failure mode, and the raise is what makes it one. Keeping it,
because it is also what surfaced this within one session rather than silently
losing a metric — but the blast radius is now guarded by a test rather than by
nobody.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): announce the renderer toggle, and count tokens the le…
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): announce the renderer toggle, and count tokens the legacy path has

Two defects a legacy session exposed, one in the feature and one in the telemetry
that was supposed to observe it.

Ctrl+Shift+L switched engines silently. Every other toggle here announces —
hover auto-pause, overlay visibility — and this one's only tell on screen is that
the legacy renderer paints a semi-transparent background box behind the cue,
which a user has to already know to look for and which says nothing at all if
they were already on legacy. The reducer now names the engine it is moving TO,
which needs `legacy_forced` among the session inputs.

`subtitle_draw` counted `len(request.boxes)`. The legacy renderer produces its
own boxes rather than consuming measured ones, so that reads 0 on exactly the
path the span was added to make visible: a field trace carried `tokens=0` for all
33 legacy draws. It now counts the tokenizer's own tokens, which both engines
have, and keeps the measured-box count as its own attribute.

Field evidence from that session (33 draws, one episode, legacy throughout):

    subtitle_draw[path=legacy]   p50  6.96 ms   p95 15.70   max 17.93

with `subtitle.renderer_forced[renderer=legacy]=1` confirming the toggle fired,
and the ladder spans correctly absent — the legacy renderer colors the cue
itself, so no device ever runs.

entry.title: feat(bench): split the extraction that is 99% of a geometry render
entry.content:
feat(bench): split the extraction that is 99% of a geometry render

`extract_ms` was one number covering ~99% of a libasslite render — libass's own
render is 0.065 ms against 11.5 ms here — so it said "the slow part is ours",
which nobody can act on. Split four ways it names a function.

Measured (M3 Pro, 24 tokens, 1920x1080, 40 reps):

    owners map alloc    0.111 ms    1.0%
    collect layers     11.191 ms   97.0%
    validate tokens     0.011 ms    0.1%
    coverage masks      3.987 ms   (demoted path only)

So `_collect_layer` is the whole answer: a per-pixel Python loop over
`enumerate(layer.bitmap)`, running once per painted pixel of every glyph.

The frame-sized owner map is NOT the problem, which is worth recording because
its size argues otherwise — `array("H")` over 1920x1080 is 4 MB zeroed per cue,
and it costs 1%. Timed apart precisely because it scales with the FRAME while the
collect loop scales with the INK, and one number could not tell those apart.

`coverage masks` reads 0 unless the snapshot keeps them, which happens only after
a face is demoted to the raster device — so it is measured on its own request
rather than left looking free. It is a second per-pixel pass over the same layers
and adds ~35% to the extraction when it runs.

The split arrives through the backend's existing `GeometryTelemetry` port, and
the parameter is optional, so every current caller and the package's public API
are unchanged.

entry.title: feat(bench): price each color device and each renderer apart
entry.content:
feat(bench): price each color device and each renderer apart

`cue_redraw` timed all three legs of a colored cue as one number, so two
questions had no answer: whether the raster device is dear next to the text one,
and whether the measuring or the drawing renderer dominates. A session read
libasslite at p50 31.7 ms against cue_redraw at 2.1 ms, which reads as a verdict
and is not one — different jobs at different rates, one of them instrumented.

Measured on one synthetic cue, per token, so the numbers divide (M3 Pro, 24
tokens, 40 reps):

    ladder classify           0.049 ms
    device 1 overprint        3.85 us/token
    device 2 overpaint       18.25 us/token
    device 3 decoration       0.020 ms delta
    legacy renderer         436.1  us/token
    libasslite              528.1  us/token   (99.1% our extraction)

So the device ladder is microseconds and the renderers are hundreds of them: the
two are not in the same conversation, and within libasslite it is our extraction
to optimise, not libass, whose render is 0.11 ms.

The libasslite split comes through the backend's own `GeometryTelemetry` port
rather than a wrapper, so it is exact rather than inferred from the outside.

mpv's OSD leg is deliberately absent — a `compute_bounds` round trip into another
process cannot be measured headlessly, and `saitenka.subtitle.calibration_ms`
records it in a live session instead. A number here covering it would be the
wall-clock proxy BENCHMARKS.md warns against.

Both device legs assert they did work before reporting. The first draft sized
48x48 coverage masks for 120x48 boxes; `TokenMask.usable` rejected every one,
`compose` returned None, and device 2 came out the CHEAPEST leg at 1.77 us/token
for compositing nothing. Tests pin both guards and the absent-libass case, which
must read as not-measured rather than as free.

entry.title: feat(telemetry): price the color ladder and the three renderers separ…
entry.content:
feat(telemetry): price the color ladder and the three renderers separately

Three questions the trace could not answer, each because the cost of a cue was
one number covering everything.

WHICH ENGINE RAN. `subtitle_renderer_forced` counts the switch, once, so a
session that drew every cue on the legacy renderer and one that never touched it
differed by a single event — and neither carried what a draw cost. `subtitle_draw`
wraps the dispatch with path=native|legacy|suspended|unowned.

WHICH DEVICE COST WHAT. Device 1 emits ASS events, device 2 composites pixels,
and `cue_redraw` lumped both into one duration, so "is the raster expensive?"
had no answer. `subtitle_overprint_build` carries the device split and the event
count; `subtitle_overpaint_compose` carries mask count and composited area —
each leg reporting the quantity its own cost scales with.

The event count is also the only signal that says whether a spaced token split
per glyph. The split events carry no `\fsp`, so a payload signature cannot tell
"split" from "never spaced"; events exceeding tokens can.

WHAT THE OSD LEG COSTS. `compute_bounds` makes mpv lay the payload out on its
core thread and was untimed — `subtitle_layout_drift` spans the arithmetic after
the answer arrives, which is microseconds. Timed from before the submit, because
the queue wait ahead of it is part of what the stall costs.

Without that last one every span in the draw path measured our side only, which
made the measuring renderer look expensive purely by being the one instrumented:
a real session reads libasslite at p50 31.7 ms against cue_redraw at 2.1 ms, and
97.4% of the libasslite figure is our extraction rather than libass.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): key the calibration on weight and slant, and pin the …
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): key the calibration on weight and slant, and pin the accept band

Second adversarial review, on the artifact rather than the story.

`payload_signature` matched only `\fn…\fs…`, so a payload differing only by
`\b1` was the same question. Weight and slant select a different font FILE, so
a cached "agrees" earned by the regular run suppressed the check on the bold
one — whose substituted bold face is the exact class this module exists to
catch, and the one no user can report. The run tags are in the key now.

`_effective_run_style` recomputed the reset target from the event's style,
ignoring an earlier `\rStyle`. `{\rBolded\b}` came back regular while libass
drew it bold, and `{\rBolded\fsp}` took the wrong style's spacing.

`\b` followed libass only approximately. `ass_parse.c` resets to the style for a
bare tag AND for any value outside {0, 1} ∪ [100, ∞) — so `\b2` on a bold style
is bold, not regular. Same for `\i`, where anything but 0 or 1 resets.

`TILE_PADDING_PX` was pinned by nothing: 24 kept the whole suite green while
leaving the accept band one pixel from the 29 px class. What matters is the band
(`TILE_PADDING_PX + DRIFT_EPSILON_PX`), squeezed from both sides, so both ends
are asserted against named constants — the measured padding ceiling below and
the substituted-face class above. A second sweep (5760 unclipped bitmaps, sizes
12–299) puts that ceiling at 17, not the 16 one tile implies, so the docstring
now leads with the measurement and cites the tile only as the mechanism.

Four tests passed regardless of the logic they named, and now do not: the `\b`
prefix guard (every case resolved to regular either way — it needed a run that
starts bold), the `glyph_dy` arithmetic (every fixture y was equal, so the sign
was free), and the `ScaleX`/`Italic` style-row reads (the fixture's values were
the fallbacks, so the lookup could point at a nonexistent column). Each was
confirmed by mutating the source and watching only the intended test go red.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): refuse glyph offsets that do not count the token's gl…
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): refuse glyph offsets that do not count the token's glyphs

Adversarial review found three defects in the per-glyph work.

`event_lines` indexed `glyph_dx` by position in `paint.text`, but the two come
from different places: the offsets are measured against the prepared ASS surface
and cached under it, while the text is the tokenizer's surface for whatever cue
is current. A snapshot that outlives its cue pairs them up wrong, and nothing
compared them — longer text raised `IndexError` inside the draw, shorter text
silently dropped the glyphs past its end. `drawable` now checks the counts, so
such a token routes to the raster device, which colors it correctly anyway.

`per_glyph` accepted negative spacing, because `bool(-2.0)` is true. Tight
typesetting overlaps its glyphs, and the probe tells them apart by color — an
ambiguous pixel makes the backend refuse the whole render, so a single
negative-spacing cue cost every token in the batch its anchor. Positive spacing
only; a tight token draws whole, exactly as it did before this work.

The device census counted inside `color_ladder`, which a drawn cue builds three
times (overpaint image, payload, calibration probe). The counter read two or
three times the cue's tokens, by a factor that moved with the calibration
cadence. The ladder now carries the devices and the count is taken at the one
call site that means "this cue was drawn".

Also notes on `subtitle.layout_drift_px` that its values are not comparable
across the tile-padding discount.

entry.title: test(subtitles): build the differential's WordBox by name, not position
entry.content:
test(subtitles): build the differential's WordBox by name, not position

`our_word_boxes` rebuilt the runtime snapshot with a positional argument list.
Every `WordBox` field past the rect has a default, so a short list is silently
legal — and this helper has dropped a newly added field three times (`text`,
then the run metrics, then `glyph_dx`).

Each time the token reached the assertion carrying a default the runtime would
never have produced, so the oracle reported a product failure whose traceback
pointed nowhere near the helper that caused it.

Building the dict from `fields(WordBox)` makes the next added field an
`AttributeError` at the source instead.

entry.title: feat(telemetry): count which device drew each token, and why a hover …
entry.content:
feat(telemetry): count which device drew each token, and why a hover missed

Device 1 was dead in production for weeks without a meter moving. Every existing
signal was negative — no demotions, no errors — and the raster fallback colours
the cue correctly, so "device 1 drew nothing" and "device 1 drew everything"
produced identical telemetry and an identical picture.

`subtitle.token_device` counts the fork positively, per token, so the primary
rung's share is readable rather than inferred from the absence of complaints.

`hover.target_outcomes` splits what a `Cancel` used to flatten: a cursor that
missed the word, a cue with no tokens, and a cue whose tokens carry no geometry
are three different faults that all read as one silent no-op.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): reproduce the run the overprint measured, glyph by glyph
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): reproduce the run the overprint measured, glyph by glyph

Device 1 redraws a token as its own `\an7\pos`-ed event, and that event has to
land where the token already is. Two things stopped it.

The payload dropped the run's layout properties. `Spacing`, `ScaleX`, `Bold` and
`Italic` were measured but never re-emitted, so the redraw was shaped from a
different run than the one it was correcting for. They now travel from the style
catalogue through the geometry contract to the event, resolved per token —
`\fscx` and `\fsp` are routinely toggled mid-line — and are omitted from the tags
when they hold libass's default, so a cue that overrides none produces the same
payload bytes it did before.

The rest is mpv's, not ours: it holds two libass instances, and they segment
shaping runs differently. libass starts a new run at every glyph of a run
carrying letter spacing, but only while `whole_text_layout` is off, and that flag
is derived from the style's `Encoding`. mpv's subtitle style keeps the authored
encoding — LTR, flag off, runs split per glyph — while its OSD style is
`Encoding = -1` (`sub/osd_libass.c`), which resolves to `FRIBIDI_PAR_ON` and
turns the flag implicitly on, so the OSD shapes the whole token as one run.

The resulting advances differ per glyph pair (1.42 px and 1.77 px on the first
two glyphs of one four-glyph token, 0 on the rest), so no scalar corrects it. A
token that is both multi-glyph and spaced is therefore drawn one event per glyph:
a lone glyph is a single shaping run in either instance. The probe measures each
glyph twice — inside its token and drawn alone — and carries the difference as
`glyph_dx`. Unspaced tokens are untouched and stay a single event.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): stop the padding allowance swallowing the drift it mu…
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): stop the padding allowance swallowing the drift it must catch

The calibration verdict discounts a positive right/bottom drift as libass tile
allocation rather than layout, because `compute_bounds` answers with a union of
bitmap rectangles and libass rounds each one out to a tile on those two edges.
The allowance was set to 32 px — the tile size of a `CONFIG_LARGE_TILES` build.

Both meson and autoconf default that option OFF, so a tile is 16 px
(`ass_bitmap_engine.c`: `tile_order = 5` only under the flag, else 4). Measured
across 45 run×size combinations against the installed mpv: worst right 15,
worst bottom 16, and single-glyph boxes come back as exact multiples of 16.

At 32 the allowance reached past the class it exists to separate. A substituted
face reads 29 px on one edge; with the discount at 32 that scored 0, so every
positive drift up to 36 px read as agreement and the verdict was switched off
for its own motivating case, silently, with every gate green.

The sign of that 29 is not settled — 0e13cca4 wrote −29 in prose and +29 in the
two tests it added — so the scoring is now pinned in both directions rather than
resting on a reading of the record, and the gap between the allowance and the
signal is asserted so the two numbers cannot drift apart unnoticed.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): key anchors by event, normalize the probed text, reme…
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): key anchors by event, normalize the probed text, remember failures

Second review pass. None of the three fires through today's producer, and each
is inside a contract the package already states.

The offset was looked up by token index alone. `_validate_palette` requires only
the (event, index) PAIR to be unique, so two events in one frame both answer to
index 0 — a frame with two events routinely has two first tokens — and the last
one measured hands its correction to the other word. Keyed by both now.

`_token_surface` sliced the raw text while every offset in that module is
defined against the normalized form (`\r` dropped, literal `\N` folded to one
newline). Past a break, every token read one character late and probed a
neighbour's string.

A probe that measures nothing is not retried forever. `extract_token_geometry`
refuses a palette colour that drew nothing, so one inkless token — text the
overprint would refuse anyway — fails the whole batch; with nothing recording
the attempt, the batch re-rendered once per geometry render for the session.

Smaller, from the same pass: the probe renders under the cue's own style, since
hinting and blur change a glyph's extent and measuring without them returns an
offset for a render nobody performs; at timestamp 0, since its events start
there and a long file would silently draw nothing; probe renderers evict
most-recently-used last like the cue's; and the row pitch is imported rather
than restated beside the frame it has to agree with.

`fragments`' docstring claimed extent-based routing to the raster device. That
is not implemented — `Fragment.matches` exists so the decision has a measurement
to stand on, and the docstring now says which of the two it is.

The first of these had a test that could not fail: it gave the two events
different token indices, so index-only keying passed it. Planting the defect is
what showed that, not reading it.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): bound the anchor cache and cover the probe wiring
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): bound the anchor cache and cover the probe wiring

Review findings on the anchor fix, both real.

The cache was unbounded, and its key is not stable the way its docstring
claimed. The size in it is the FRAME's, not the document's — `_palette_in_frame
_units` multiplies by `frame_height / play_res_y` — so dragging a window edge
mints a distinct float per pixel of height, every one of them a miss, every miss
a second libass render, and none of it ever reclaimed. "A repeated cue costs a
dict lookup" holds while the window is still and nowhere else. Now LRU, bounded,
and the comment says which case the bound is for.

The wiring had no coverage outside the `live` tier, which does not run in CI. A
wrong sign, a key that never matches, or a probe failing forever would all have
shipped green: the unit tests covered the pure arithmetic in `fragments` and
nothing that decides whether it is reached. Six tests over the backend probe —
offset carried, unprobed token left alone, measured once per cue, the cue's
renderer never pointed at a probe document, probe renderers closed, cache
bounded — and two over the subtraction itself in `test_overprint`.

Writing them exposed a fake that answered the cue's palette whatever document it
was handed, which made the probe's own colours unrecoverable and hid the whole
path behind the swallowed exception below. It answers the document now.

That exception no longer swallows silently: the first failure logs at warning,
since a probe that never succeeds disables the correction for the session with
nothing on screen to show it, and the rest stay at debug so a bad face cannot
flood the log.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): anchor the overprint where the token's ink actually l…
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): anchor the overprint where the token's ink actually lands

`\an7` positions the line box; a measured box is ink. Passing the ink origin to
`\pos` planted every redraw an ascent-gap low — 39% of the colour on the glyphs,
the rest on empty frame, with mpv's own subtitle showing through above it.

The offset cannot be derived from the box (libass reports no baseline) and is
not a constant: it depends on the token's tallest glyph, so it differs per word
in the same cue. It is measured instead, by rendering the fragmented layout the
overprint will ask for through the renderer that produced the boxes, and reading
where each token's ink lands.

    39% -> 99.9% of the overprint on a glyph mpv drew

Cost is one probe render per unseen (text, face, size). A repeated cue, a redraw,
and a recurring word all cost a dict lookup; a session's second and third render
of the same cue probe nothing. The probe uses its own renderer per font
environment so it never evicts the cue document from the renderer drawing the
cue, and a probe that fails leaves the offsets unrecorded — every redraw keeps
the origin it had before, which is today's behaviour.

The live oracle now drives `overprint_payload` rather than assembling paints
itself: the placement under test is a decision `_assign_rung` makes, and a test
that re-implements it would have kept passing while the shipped path was wrong.
That is not hypothetical — this commit's first two attempts passed the anchor
through a palette that dropped the text and through a field order that put
`coverage` into `anchor_dx`, and only the end-to-end pixel count caught either.
